title: Iran Demands Trump Choose War or Diplomacy as Talks Set to Resume This Week – Live Updates
body:
The United States and Iran appear poised for a new round of diplomatic overtures even as the conflict that erupted seven months ago shows no sign of abating, prompting President Donald Trump to publicly assert that talks will resume this week. Tehran, however, has offered a proposal that many U.S. lawmakers deem insufficient, and the president’s remarks have been met with sharp criticism from Republican senators who warn that the administration is giving the impression that war is an acceptable fallback. The stakes are high: the ongoing hostilities have already disrupted global oil markets, threatened navigation through the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz, and heightened regional tensions across the Middle East.

Trump’s comments, made during an interview with Axios, suggested that both sides are “ready to get back to the table” despite the fact that neither side has signaled any willingness to soften its core demands. The United States continues to press Iran for a complete cessation of its support for proxy militias in Iraq, Syria, and Yemen, as well as a rollback of its nuclear enrichment program. Tehran, in turn, insists on the lifting of U.S. sanctions and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to commercial traffic—a lifeline for the world’s oil supply that has been intermittently blocked by Iranian missile strikes and naval confrontations.

Republican Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana, a vocal critic of the president’s approach, dismissed Iran’s latest proposal as “not a serious offer.” Kennedy argued that the plan, which ostensibly includes a limited reopening of the strait and a vague commitment to resume negotiations, fails to address the fundamental issues of Iranian aggression and nuclear ambition. “The president’s not Bambi’s baby brother,” Kennedy said, implying that Trump’s diplomatic overtures could be interpreted as a tacit endorsement of Iranian brinkmanship. Other members of the GOP, while generally supportive of a strong stance against Tehran, expressed concern that the administration’s messaging might embolden Iran to continue its pressure campaign in the Gulf.

Analysts note that the timing of the proposed talks coincides with a sharp rise in oil prices, as the market reacts to the uncertainty surrounding the strait’s accessibility. The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world’s petroleum passes, has been a flashpoint since the conflict began, with Iranian forces targeting tankers and U.S. naval vessels. A credible Iranian offer to reopen the waterway, even partially, could alleviate some of the economic pressure, but experts warn that any agreement would need robust verification mechanisms to ensure compliance on both sides.

The diplomatic landscape is further complicated by internal politics in Iran. Hardliners within the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have repeatedly warned that any concession on sanctions or nuclear matters would be seen as a betrayal of revolutionary principles. Conversely, moderate elements in Tehran’s foreign ministry have been pushing for a de‑escalation path that could restore Iran’s access to the global financial system. The United States, meanwhile, faces its own domestic challenges, with the upcoming midterm elections sharpening partisan divides over foreign policy and defense spending.

If talks do resume this week, the negotiations are likely to be preliminary, focusing on confidence‑building measures such as a limited ceasefire in the Gulf and a mutually agreed framework for further discussions on the nuclear issue. The outcome will hinge on whether Washington can extract tangible concessions from Tehran without appearing to capitulate to Iranian pressure, and whether Tehran can present a plan that satisfies U.S. demands for denuclearization and regional stability. 

Looking ahead, the next few weeks will test the resilience of diplomatic channels amid a conflict that has already cost lives and disrupted global trade. A successful restart of negotiations could pave the way for a broader settlement that eases tensions in the Middle East and stabilizes oil markets. Conversely, a failure to bridge the gaps may push both sides closer to a protracted confrontation, with far‑reaching implications for international security and the global economy.
